claim: Worked examples give novice human learners a medium average gain in maths (g=0.48, 181 effect sizes, 55 studies), but heterogeneity is huge (I2 about 94 percent; 41 of 185 interim effect sizes were negative).
agent_test: Compare agent with and without a stored solved case on each problem class; report per-class effect, not one average.

claim: The effect is strongest for novices and fades, then reverses, as expertise rises (expertise reversal).
agent_test: Run each class at several agent strengths or after N successes; find the class-level cross-over where the example stops helping.
note: Pooled anchor: Tetzlaff 2025 meta-analysis d=0.505 for high assistance at low prior knowledge, d=-0.428 at high prior knowledge (176 effects, 60 studies, N=5,924; seen in snippets only). Agent side is mixed: SkillsBench gains did not shrink for stronger models (d09) but memory damage grew with baseline (d12).

claim: For strong LLMs, generic exemplars add nothing over zero-shot reasoning once answer parsing is fixed (GSM8K Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct: 8-shot 95.75, zero-shot 91.58, zero-shot-fixed 95.83); exemplars mostly align format. This is the machine form of expertise reversal.
agent_test: At equal tokens: arm A zero-shot, arm B one retrieved example, with the same fixed answer parser. Gate on zero-shot pass rate.
note: Agreeing results: ThinkRetrieve static in-context examples (k=3) do not beat standard thinking on AIME 2025 (Qwen3-4B 62.2 vs 63.3; 8B 66.7 vs 67.8); WebArena unconditional retrieval -1.9 and +1.7 pp; Dynamic Cheatsheet gives R1 and o1 minimal gains. Holds for generic or static examples; relevance-matched in-trace retrieval helps small reasoning models (K25).

claim: For reasoning-trained models, adding retrieved teacher solutions lowers accuracy (AIME25 one demo -6 to -16 points, three demos up to -35), because the model copies steps; converting demos into explicit insights first repairs it (I2S: GPT-4.1 34.0 to 48.0 on AIME25; R1-Distill-14B 50 to 54).
agent_test: Compare raw example in context versus example distilled to an insight line, at equal prompt tokens.

claim: In human studies the worked-example advantage fails to appear when text and diagram are split (split attention) or the diagram is self-sufficient (redundancy); integrating restores it. Implication: stored examples must be self-contained and minimal.
agent_test: Ablate entries that refer to missing context against self-contained versions; ablate prose that restates steps.

claim: Exemplar content correctness matters less than relevance and step order in LLMs: invalid reasoning in CoT demos keeps about 81 percent of CoT accuracy (GSM8K 39.5 vs 48.5, standard 15.4); irrelevant demos fall to 11.0.
agent_test: Seed library with a deliberately flawed but relevant case versus a polished irrelevant case; measure.

claim: Numeric values in demonstrations are load-bearing even if structure dominates; wrong values hurt more than wrong operator order.
agent_test: Corrupt numbers versus order in stored cases and measure the drop.

claim: One well-matched example is about as good as many, and one known-correct demo beats using all eight (about 83 versus 60 percent on GSM8K, code-davinci-002); adding more demos can interfere. Humans: Reed and Bolstad found two contrasting examples beat one (65 versus 38 percent) and Quilici and Mayer found three no better than one for categorisation.
agent_test: Sweep k=0,1,2,4 retrieved cases at equal total tokens (shorter cases for larger k).
note: Diversity paper (Llama-3.1-8B, K=4): GSM8K flat across selection methods (65.30 to 66.92); diversity helps on harder non-reasoning tasks (GeoQuery 62.79 to 71.14). Contrast versus retrieval match for reasoning is still untested.

claim: The 'few beats many' rule is task-specific: for many-label classification, performance keeps rising to thousands of demos (+36.8 points on average 10 to 1000), and for MATH plain ICL peaks near 125 examples.
agent_test: Do not apply a k cap to label-mapping subtasks; test separately.

claim: Adding self-explanation prompts to worked examples does not help in the maths meta-analysis and in a 2026 classroom trial (fading 1.08 vs fading+SE 0.93, pre-post g); older training studies found large self-explanation effects (about 2 SD). Human evidence on prompts is split.
agent_test: Equal-token test: example alone versus example plus a one-line goal-and-reason per step.
note: LLM judge can grade self-explanations (F1 .91, N=8 pilot); effect of self-explanation on the explainer at different strengths remains untested.

claim: For LLMs, a reflect-on-the-example step helps only if the model is strong enough to use it: LEAP gains on GPT-4 DROP 72.05 to 79.55 but Llama-2-70B GSM8K 52.5 to 50.6.
agent_test: Run the self-explain operator at two model sizes with equal tokens.

claim: Fading (removing late steps progressively) beat plain worked examples in a 2026 classroom trial (N=114, fading g=1.08 vs worked example+SE 0.32 vs problems 0.24, within-condition pre-post) and fading suits near transfer; far transfer needs principle-naming prompts.
agent_test: Backward-fade library entries: full, last step blank, last two blank; compare with full-only at equal tokens.

claim: Partial and full examples do not reliably match: completion examples equalled or beat full ones (Paas, Stark) but full solutions beat partial formats for novice maths feedback (Manson and Ayres).
agent_test: Full versus step-blanked case for a class the agent has failed versus mastered.
note: Paas 1992 abstract: worked arm best, completion second, conventional worst (abstract only). LLM prefix scaffold (Shepherding, Llama-3.2-3B GSM8K): accuracy rises 77.5 to 94.1 as the given share of the solution grows 0 to 90 percent.

claim: Alternating examples with problems matches or beats example-only study when problems carry tutor-like feedback; the pure example advantage can disappear into an efficiency gain (stoichiometry: 21 percent less time, no learning difference; SQL-Tutor: example-only worst).
agent_test: Compare example-only versus attempt-with-verifier versus alternate, at equal tokens, and report tokens to solve.

claim: Example-first ordering beats problem-first in worked-example research (example-then-problem over problem-then-example).
agent_test: Order test: retrieved case before attempt versus after a failed attempt.

claim: The effect extends beyond algorithmic domains in humans (legal reasoning; primary science argumentation) but evidence is thin and mostly secondary.
agent_test: Test library on ARC (algorithmic) versus an open-ended task.
note: Nievelstein 2013 abstract (law, novice and advanced): worked example effect for both, no reversal. Abstract only; no numbers.

claim: LLM agents that store verified, abstracted past solutions gain most on compositional or distant tasks: Voyager (skill library; zero-shot unseen tasks 19 vs 36 iterations on diamond pickaxe), Agent Workflow Memory (WebArena 35.5, +12.0 points, +51.1 percent relative; gain 8.9 to 14.0 points as train-test gap grows), Buffer of Thoughts, ExpeL.
agent_test: Library on/off at equal tokens, stratified by task depth and by train-test distance.
note: Library gains are real for curated or verified skills (SkillsBench +16.3 pp mean, 40.6 vs 24.3; Dynamic Cheatsheet AIME24 23.3 to 50.0) but self-written skills give none (21.0 vs 24.3) and SkillEvolBench finds static curated skills hurt 7 of 10 models and raw trajectories beat distilled skills.

claim: Storing wrong solutions is the main risk: AWM authors warn incorrect workflows degrade performance; Voyager stores only after self-verification; positive-demo selection decides accuracy.
agent_test: Inject 0, 10, 30 percent wrong entries into the library and measure the slope.
note: Measured now: add-all memory loses 3.7 to 12.1 points against a small fixed memory while a strict evaluator gains 4 to 22 points (d13); wrong hints cost 6.8 points vs +2.6 for right ones (d17); conflicting memory costs up to 26 points and damage grows with baseline (d12). No slope against percent wrong yet.

claim: Contrast pairs of a wrong and a right answer with no explanation beat explained or CoT prompts in 85 to 88 percent of model x dataset x task combinations (editing +4.4, labelling F1 +5.6 over CoT), and incorrect examples in human preschoolers were as useful as correct ones.
agent_test: Library entries: clean solution versus wrong/right pair, equal tokens.

claim: Model-written solved cases can replace human-written ones: Reinforced ICL plateaus near 25 examples about 5 points above ground-truth ICL on MATH500; self-generated exemplars add 1 to 3 points on GSM8K for GPT-3.5.
agent_test: Fill the library from the agent's own verified solutions and compare to hand-written.

claim: Unrestricted solution access harms later unaided performance: GPT Base students scored 17 percent worse on the later exam without GPT, while a hint-only tutor removed the harm.
agent_test: Agent attempts first; reveal the case only on failure; compare to always showing the case.

claim: Part of the worked-example effect may be a format or efficiency effect rather than learning (McLaren time cut, Min et al. format/label-space, Cheng format alignment, Madaan symbols and patterns).
agent_test: Always include a format-only exemplar arm and a fixed parser.
note: SkillsBench authors say gains may partly reflect more context rather than procedure.

claim: Founding result, checked against the paper (Sweller and Cooper 1985, Exps 2-5, N=20/22/40/24): studying worked examples took a fraction of the learning time (Exp 3 first-presentation 32.0 s vs 185.5 s, ratio 5.8) and gave faster, more accurate solutions on test problems of the same structure (Exp 3 43.6 vs 78.1 s, errors 0.18 vs 1.64; Exp 5 time-matched 52.4 vs 101.1 s). Exp 2 showed no significant test-time gain (105.4 vs 127.1 s) and errors only p=.10.
agent_test: Report solve cost (tokens, steps) and accuracy separately for study-then-solve vs solve; expect a cost gap first, an accuracy gap only on same-structure items.
note: Earlier text said the effect failed in geometry and kinematics until split attention was removed; that is not in the 1985 paper and rests on other sources (a20, b04). One lab, nonparametric tests, small cells.

claim: Sweller and Cooper (1985) found no far-transfer benefit: on test problems with new structure but the same algebra, worked-example and conventional groups did not differ (Exp 4 62.6 vs 59.8 s; Exp 5 163.7 vs 183.3 s), and interpolating dissimilar problems erased the advantage on similar ones. The effect is specific to the structure studied.
agent_test: Test every library class on near-structure and new-structure items; expect gain only on near. Check that interposing unrelated items between study and test removes it.

claim: Retrieved solved cases help LLMs when they match structure and arrive at the point of need, and mostly when the model is small: ThinkRetrieve in-trace retrieval on AIME 2025 gives +13.4 points over sequential TTS at 1.7B but about +2 at 4B and 8B (66.7 vs 64.4; 71.1 vs 68.9); random retrieval gives part of the gain; static prefix examples give none.
agent_test: Compare prefix examples, after-stall retrieval, and random retrieval at equal tokens on items the agent fails zero-shot.

claim: Entry form (full solution, skeleton, abstraction level, one worked example inside a skill) matters less than availability and correctness in the controlled tests so far: abstraction and one-example effects are inside +-7 pp with intervals crossing zero (SkillsBench subset, 30 tasks, 2 models), while raw-versus-distilled results conflict (Dynamic Cheatsheet: distilled 50.0 vs full history 26.7 on AIME24; SkillEvolBench: raw retrieved trajectories beat distilled skills).
agent_test: Three-arm test at equal tokens: full solved case, skeleton plus case, abstract insight; same retrieval, same verifier, ARC-like and open-ended items.

claim: Partial-solution scaffolds help weaker models monotonically with the share given (Llama-3.2-3B GSM8K 77.5, 81.1, 81.7, 85.4, 89.8, 94.1 at 0, 10, 30, 50, 70, 90 percent prefix). No LLM test of backward fading as a teaching device exists in what was found.
agent_test: Run fading only on items the agent fails; compare full case, completion (blank last steps) and prefix at equal tokens.

claim: Hint and memory quality asymmetry: a wrong or irrelevant hint costs about 2.5 times what a right one gains (MATH, 11 models: 0.5355 baseline, 0.5615 correct, 0.4674 adversarial, 0.4628 random); base models lose even with a correct hint.
agent_test: Set the store threshold on precision; report the break-even share of wrong entries.

claim: Element-interactivity gating has a direction but no size: worked example effect for high interactivity and generation effect for low, flipping with expertise (Chen, Kalyuga and Sweller 2015-2016), but no means, F values or N were retrieved and no agent-side classifier of interactivity has been tested.
agent_test: Label items by number of interacting steps; test skip-versus-show by label.
